published_by: Ofgem (Default Tariff Cap) + HM Government (Energy Price Guarantee)
what_this_is: THE LAW, NOT A READING OF IT. The published cap-window boundaries and the published typical-household unit rates for each window, plus the EPG overlay where it was in force. Nothing here interprets the law: no carry-forward rule, no min() selection, no segment filter, no basis conversion. Those are READINGS and each lane owns its own.

basis.conversion: p/kWh x 10 = GBP/MWh. The p/kWh is the GB-average typical-household unit rate, i.e. (benchmark-consumption allowance minus nil-consumption allowance) / the benchmark consumption for that period -- Ofgem's own construction.
basis.vat: INCLUDING VAT, AND THE RATE IS NOT ALWAYS 5%. Gas is 5% throughout. ELECTRICITY IS ZERO-RATED FROM 2026-10-01 TO 2027-03-31 under the Government's announcement, so the 2026-10-01 electricity row is inclusive of 0% and equals its ex-VAT value. A reader dividing any row here by 1.05 to recover an ex-VAT figure is wrong for that row.
basis.standing_charge: EXCLUDED - this is a unit-rate ceiling only (R14: the basis travels with the figure)
basis.benchmark_consumption: NOT A CONSTANT, and it is the divisor behind every figure here. Electricity single-rate: 3,100 kWh to 2025-12-31, 2,700 from 2026-01-01, 2,500 from 2026-07-01. Gas: 11,500 kWh to 2026-06-30, 9,500 from 2026-07-01. Ofgem's published cap tables state the divisor on their face -- '(2,700kWh)' on the 15b table and '(2,500kWh)' on the 17a table -- which is how the two 2026 bases are corroborated rather than inferred.
basis.per_row_source: Every window carries `source`. That is not decoration: `ofgem_cap_unit_rate_composition` cross-checks ITS derivation against this artefact, and a row derived from the same cap level model cannot corroborate a derivation from that model. Rows marked "ofgem_default_tariff_cap_level_model_v1.31" are EXCLUDED from that cross-check by name.

window_boundaries_source: https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/energy-regulation/domestic-and-non-domestic/energy-pricing-rules/energy-price-cap/energy-price-cap-default-tariff-levels - six-monthly Apr/Oct from 1 Jan 2019 through 30 Sep 2022, quarterly from 1 Oct 2022
unit_rate_source: Published typical-household p/kWh per cap period (electricityprices.org.uk cap history). The Oct-2021 20.8p/4.07p and Apr-2022 28.34p/7.37p levels are independently corroborated by House of Commons Library CBP-9714 ('20.8p -> 28.3p electricity, 4.1p -> 7.4p gas'). Full sourcing: docs/market_research/ofgem_cap_windows.md
epg_note: Between Oct-2022 and Jun-2023 the Energy Price Guarantee held a typical dual-fuel bill at GBP 2,500, well below the Ofgem cap (which peaked at GBP 4,279 for Jan-Mar 2023). Both instruments are published separately here rather than pre-combined, so that a lane which fails to notice the EPG is a lane that MISREAD the law rather than a lane that was handed a different law.
r13_wall: Every date and level here is real published regulatory history, sourced blind to company P&L. No value in this file may be moved because a simulation result looks wrong.
portability: A schedule of windows, not a set of year branches. A second market or a changed regime supplies its own artefact behind the same loaders.

source_check.publication: Ofgem 'Energy price cap: default tariff levels' -- the version-history page (window boundaries), the published Benchmark Maximum Charges cap tables per charge restriction period (PDF), and the Default tariff cap level model v1.31 (the 2026 unit rates). Rows to 2025-12-31 remain on a third-party cap-history compilation, marked per row.
source_check.how_to_recheck: GET the URL above. TWO legs, and they no longer share a verdict because every row now carries its own `source`. (1) BOUNDARIES AND 2026 LEVELS: take the highest v<major>.<minor> across links matching Default[-_]tariff[-_]cap[-_]level OR Energy-price-cap-levels-pre-levelised-rates-model (the series is published under BOTH names, v1.30 under the second, so a check keyed to the filename stem misses editions). If it is above `version_token`, re-derive the rows marked ofgem_default_tariff_cap_level_model_v1.31. Ofgem announces each quarterly period about six weeks ahead, so a period beyond the last row here is a period not yet published rather than a gap. (2) THE PRE-2026 UNIT RATES, and this is still the weaker leg: they are NOT from that page but from electricityprices.org.uk's cap history, corroborated at two points against House of Commons Library CBP-9714. A third-party compilation carries no edition marker and cannot be supersession-checked at all. Re-siting them onto Ofgem's own published cap tables (one PDF per charge restriction period, linked from the same page) is the fix. THAT RE-SITING HAS A COST TO WEIGH: it would make those rows share a source with `ofgem_cap_unit_rate_composition`'s derivation, and the composition's cross-check -- the only evidence its benchmark-minus-nil decomposition is right -- would lose the 21 independent periods it currently stands on. Re-site onto the PUBLISHED CAP TABLE PDFs (a separate publication with its own rounding), never onto the model workbook.

checked_for_supersession.note: Settled from `cannot_tell` on 2026-09-07. The page was fetched (HTTP 200, 381,032 bytes) and the four cap periods it publishes beyond the previous last row -- January 2026 through October-December 2026 -- were added, derived from Ofgem's own cap level model v1.31. No later period is published; Ofgem announces about six weeks ahead. WHAT MOVED THE VERDICT IS PER-ROW PROVENANCE, not a fresher fetch. The old note said the artefact was 'only as fresh as its weakest column' and recorded cannot_tell rather than splitting the legs. Every row now carries `source`, so the legs ARE split and each can be asked separately: the 2026 rows name a versioned Ofgem edition, the rows to 2025-12-31 name the third-party compilation that still has no edition marker. Re-siting those is this artefact's remaining open job and `how_to_recheck` now names both the fix and the trap in doing it the obvious way. THE 2026 DIVISORS ARE CORROBORATED, which the finding that opened this said could not be done: Ofgem's published cap tables state the benchmark consumption on their face -- '(2,700kWh)' for period 15b, '(2,500kWh)' for 17a -- and the model's benchmark-minus-nil reproduces those PDFs to under one penny per year per region (Eastern: 717.02 vs 717.01 for 15b, 665.32 vs 665.33 for 17a). Levelisation differs between the two publications by a fixed annual amount that falls entirely in the standing charge, so it cancels out of the unit rate.
